analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "The Dash 87, Police Department of Chicago against Mosley and Greenand against Rockford. Thank you. Well, you may proceed, Mr. Barnett. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. I am the attorney for the respondent, Earl D. Mosley. This case is on certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, and it has been consolidated with the case of Greenand versus the City of Rockford, which is on appeal from the Supreme Court of Illinois. This case concerns a disorderly conduct ordinance of the City of Chicago, which prohibits all picketing on a public way within 150 feet of a primary or secondary school. The ordinance exempts from this prohibition the picketing of a school involved in a labor dispute. It became effective on April 5, 1968. Since September 1967, respondent Earl D. Mosley had picketed Jones Commercial High School located in the city of Chicago. He had simply walked on the public sidewalk adjoining Jones High School, carrying a sign which reflected his belief that Jones High School was discriminating against blacks in its admission policies and in the treatment that it afforded him. It was admitted at trial by the city that at all times Mr. Mosley's activities were peaceful, orderly, and quiet. It was further admitted at the trial by petitioners that at no time did Mr. Mosley's activities in picketing the school by himself or with a few other persons ever cause a disturbance at the school or interfere with traffic around the school. After being advised of the passage of this ordinance, Mr. Mosley contacted the Chicago Police Department and was told that he would be arrested if he continued his activities in picketing Jones. The city admitted at trial that it intended to enforce this ordinance and, in fact, Mr. Mosley would be arrested if he continued to picket the school. He then filed this declaratory judgment action, seeking a declaratory judgment and an injunction against the enforcement of this ordinance on the grounds that it violated his right to freedom of speech and that it was a violation of the Equal Protection Clause. The lower court, after a trial, held that the ordinance was constitutional. On appeal, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the ordinance on its face violated Mr. Mosley's rights to freedom of speech because the ordinance was overly broad. This ordinance is a violation of the First Amendment right to freedom of speech because it is overly broad. The vice of this ordinance is that it sweeps within its prohibition protected free speech, such as the quiet, peaceful picketing of respondent Mr. Mosley. In fact, Mr. Mosley engaged in almost the identical activity as that engaged in by Mr. Thornhill in the case of Thornhill v. Alabama some 30 years ago. This court has held that peaceful picketing is protected free speech, and the state can regulate only the abuses of picketing, which has been articulated as a test of the regulation of the manner of picketing or the purpose of picketing when there is something in the manner or purpose which gives grounds for the disallowance of that picketing. What about place? If the court pleads thee, at no time have I been able to find any decision of the court which has stated that place and place alone is sufficient to permit the regulation of picketing. It must be coupled with something in the manner of picketing or the purpose of picketing which would give grounds for the disallowance of that picketing. Do you think the statute can prohibit you from picketing where you're standing? Period. Well, I would say, Your Honor, that that statute would be lawful. But, Your Honor, the difference between that case and this case is that we have picketing here on a public way which in no way which prohibits the respondent in this case from lawfully and legitimately exercising his right to freedom of speech. The ordinance which Your Honor or the statute which Your Honor would propose I think would be attached to some legitimate state concern. All I'm trying to say is I think you'll put too much baggage on your train, that's all I was. Are you familiar with, I think it's Title 18, Section 1501 that forbids picketing on the sidewalk around this building? I am not familiar with that statute, Your Honor. I am familiar with the court sanctioning of the statute in Cox v. Louisiana which prohibited the picketing of a courthouse with the intent to influence the administration of justice. That's the same statute. That statute, Your Honor, as the court noted in the Cox case, was one which specifically dealt with a purpose of picketing. And the court found in that case that the purpose was legitimate, could legitimately be regulated by the state because the state had a legitimate interest in protecting courts from the undue influence and the interference with the administration of justice. The problem with the City of Chicago ordinance is it is not a narrowly drafted enactment that's aimed specifically at some evil, some abuse of picketing. Well, if this statute had it as a... Is this statute or an ordinance? It's an ordinance, Your Honor. It's an ordinance. If this ordinance had it as a... No one would put it in a 153 to the school for the purpose of this helping school. Right. Do you think that would become a little constitutional? I think that statute may be constitutional, Your Honor. They would have... The City would then be put to proof at a trial in that case that it was the intent of the person to disrupt the school. I'd want to say your words were for the purpose of it... For the purpose of influencing the administration of school. I wouldn't think that the... That the City would have in that instance a legitimate right to be concerned with the influencing the administration of school. That's correct, Your Honor. In that case, the Court went on at great length and I'd like to note that picketing around the courthouse may cause an undue and an oppressive influence upon jurors, let us say, who are attending a trial in that particular courthouse. In the hypothetical which Your Honor posed, I would think that someone who picketed a school with the intent to influence the administration of that school to get them to, let's say, admit more blacks or to afford blacks different treatments such as Mr. Mosley's intent, that would be a legitimate concern on his part and the state would not have an overriding interest in preventing that type of conduct and that type of free speech. That's correct, rather, both means of his expressions of freedom of speech. And that is the problem with this ordinance because what Mr. Mosley was doing was exercising nothing more than protected free speech. the city admits that he never caused a disturbance or interference with the school. And yet this ordinance arbitrarily creates a 150-foot limit within which he is prevented from exercising those rights of freedom of speech. Now the city harps over and over in their brief about disturbances and disruptions around schools as a means for justifying this ordinance. But the simple answer to that is that this ordinance is not directed at disturbances, at disruptions or picketing in such a manner as to create disturbances or disruptions around schools. There's a federal statute that forbids demonstrations of any kind within either 500 feet or 1,000 feet of an embassy of a foreign country. Would you think that falls under the same ban as the argument you're making? I think the court in one of its decisions indicated that the rationale of the embassy ordinance was that for security purposes and that the government had a legitimate concern in that particular instance of protecting these types of embassies from potential violence and disruptions. Well, in this case, isn't the ordinance for the purpose and certainly does it not serve the purpose of avoiding distraction of the students from their studies? It may serve that purpose, Your Honor, but on the other hand, it brings everything within its ambition. It prohibits all types of picketing, violent and disruptive picketing as well as purely... Aren't all types of picketing prohibited under the embassy statute? They are, Your Honor, and I would have my doubts as to the constitutionality of that. As I stated, I'm not sure if that ordinance, that statute has ever been passed upon, but I think the rationale was that there was a certain legitimate concern about security around embassies. I would think, however, that if one person was peacefully picketing an embassy and wanted to pick it within the 500-foot limit, that he ought to be entitled to do so under his First Amendment rights to freedom of speech. And that is exactly what we have here in this case, for Mr. Mosley at no time caused a disturbance around the school. He at no time interfered with the administration of the school or disrupted any school activities. Mr. Barnett, does the 150-foot limit carry any weight with you? Suppose there were no limitations at all. could he picket on the schoolhouse steps? No, I think that there would be, the state would have the right to prevent people from coming on the schoolhouse property as such, certainly in the protection of students. But this ordinance is specifically drafted to be picketing within 150 feet on a public way. So that if there were no school yards on the old building yards, people from the public sidewalk, I would think that on a public sidewalk, a person should have the right to peacefully ticket and express abuse. And this court has always sanctioned the use of the public sidewalks, parks, in the recent food employees case, as areas where historically First Amendment rights to freedom of speech have been sanctioned and have been... How about the hallway in the school number? Does your honor mean that if an ordinance were drafted prohibiting picketing there? Let's assume that this ordinance were applied to someone picketing walking up and down the halls of the school with the same sign. And no showing whatsoever of any disturbance or anything else. No, I would think that the state has a legitimate... This ordinance itself I don't think could be applied in that fashion, Your Honor. Because the 150 foot limit is from the exterior of the school. All right, but assume the ordinance did say in any school building, on public property, in the school building, or within 150 feet on the street. I think that the state would have a legitimate right to prevent picketing on its property in order that it may run its school system. Well, why? Because of that. Until there's a showing of some disruption. Well, I think an outsider, Your Honor, rather than a student, that the distinction can be drawn, because certainly there may be some... It must be, though, in terms of the tendency to disrupt. I don't think the tendency... Or to distract. I don't think it's a tendency to disrupt or distract, Your Honor. I think an outsider may be prohibited from coming on school property because of a possible danger to students, a threat or some farm to students. That isn't what the ordinance says. The ordinance says you can't come on here to pick it. That's correct. And there's a lot of strangers committed on the school property for all sorts of purposes. Well, I think that those would all be connected with the school, such as a delivery man or something like that, Your Honor. But to come on school property as such inside a building to pick it I think might cause a disruption and I think the state would have a legitimate concern of protecting its students. It might cause a disruption? Yes. But I don't think that... How about the 150 feet? You're simply saying the state has any basis for saying that it might cause a disruption? No, I don't think the might cause a disruption is enough. In fact, in a recent Tinker case... Well, it is inside the school building. Well, my argument on that is twofold, Your Honor. One, it may well cause a disruption of the school activities. And secondly, I think the state is a legitimate concern in protecting the interests of students in terms of bodily harm to them from outsiders indiscriminately coming on inside school buildings. You're just saying that you're just repeating the argument in different words in terms of its tendency to disrupt the school and to impinge on the rights of students. No, Your Honor. I think it's a difference in... a qualitative difference between someone standing outside a school on a public sidewalk walking in front of that school and and between a person coming in the school where there may well be a danger of physical harm to students, which certainly the state has an interest in protecting. Well, the ordinance says you can't come in and communicate with students with a sign in the hallway of the school. That's what the ordinance says. That's correct, Mark. Well, it has nothing to do with physical things. No, the ordinance... It has to do with insulating students and faculty members or anybody else in the building from communication like this. The ordinance prohibits, Your Honor, from picketing on a public way within 150 feet of the school. Your time, of course, and you haven't said a word about anyone involved in the labor dispute could do everything that this ordinance says. This man couldn't be killed. That is correct, Mark. That's your equal protection, aren't you? Yes, it is, Your Honor. Why should someone involved in the labor dispute be allowed to do this and this man be mostly prohibitive? Yes, that is our argument. Thank you. Miss Hall? Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court? My defendant is, my client, is Richard Green. He was, he was, he participated in a demonstration. He was arrested, convicted, and fined for violating two ordinances of the city of Rockford. One of the ordinances is the same as the one in the Mosley case, involved not picketing or demonstrating within 150 feet and accepted the person picketing in support of a labor dispute. The other ordinance prohibited a person engaged in conduct wherein he willfully made or assisted in the making of a noise or diversion which disturbed or tended to disturb the peace or good order of the school session. The defendant, and we have constantly, throughout the litigation, contended that these two ordinances are both unconstitutional, that they are violative of the 14th amendment, and that it represents an interference by the state with a person's right to picket or to speak or assemble. The facts in the drainage case prior to the proceeding in this court have not been disputed. The record went up to the Supreme Court on a short record. There was no transcript of proceedings of what occurred in the trial. The motion was made before the Illinois Supreme Court. Without objection of counsel, we submitted the case on the facts as represented in the briefs which we submitted. For the first time, the city of Rockford has disputed the facts in this case, and I submit that they not only have disputed them, but they have also made misstatements of facts. I have with me a reporter of proceedings that occurred in the circuit court of the 17th Judicial Circuit in the case of the city of Rockford v. Richard Draynor. This report of proceedings was ordered by our office and at our own expense. It was not supplied by the city of Rockford. We ordered it back in November, and it was delivered to us this past Monday on January 17th. I brought this report of proceedings with me because I thought the court might be interested in seeing what the facts were in this case, since they are now apparently in dispute. Ms. Hall, as I read the opinion of the Supreme Court of Illinois, it didn't treat any factual issue. I gathered it was just an appeal on the question of whether a statute or ordinance such as this was constitutional. Would you agree that that was a correct reading, at least, of the Supreme Court of Illinois' opinion? That is true, but the Supreme Court did mention the facts in the case as they thought were relevant, and facts were set out in the brief. The Supreme Court stated in the beginning of their opinion that a demonstration was held in front of the school, West High School. Was any state law point made to the Supreme Court of Illinois that the evidence was insufficient to support the convention? None whatsoever. And you're not making any such point as that? Not at all. But the only reason I bring this record to this court's attention is that there are facts stated in the appellate's brief which are not true. Ms. Hall, are you willing to leave that with the clerk? I certainly intend to do so, and I mentioned it to Mr. Collins when I arrived at court. I mentioned to it before lunch. He said he would think about it, and after lunch he told me that he would join in the submission of this reported proceeding. And I intend to leave it with the clerk before I leave. Is it your submission that if this ordinance had said all demonstrations of 40 or more people within 150 feet of the school building are prohibited? The ordinance said that in so many words that your submission that it would be unconstitutional? Yes, Your Honor, it would be. You're not just arguing over breadth? I am arguing over breadth. Is that your fundamental position? That's the fundamental position with respect to Section 18.1i, and also we argue that 18.1i violates the Equal Protection Clause. In our particular case... But you're also saying, I think, that even if this ordinance were limited to just covering demonstrations of 40 or more people, that it would be unconstitutional? Are you saying that if the ordinance stated that 40 or more people could demonstrate on the May not, may not demonstrate? May not demonstrate. I would say it was unconstitutional. So your argument is not just over breadth. It's that this particular activity that was actually carried on may not be prohibited. That's right. What about a thousand or more? Same argument? Your Honor, I think that to try and use numbers as 150 feet and the number of people avoids the whole problem involved here. We're concerned with the interests of the state which are involved. We're concerned with what the people who are picketing are concerned about picketing. We're concerned about the effect of their conduct. Would you not agree that a thousand people milling around the entrances of the school, the access streets, would create more of a problem than one person? If an ordinance was passed which said that there could not be so many people picketing who obstructed the ingress and egress with respect to the school, who stopped traffic, who prevented people from using the public way, if that's what the ordinance said, then it would be constitutional. But there's no evidence of that here. There were 200 people in our particular instance who walked up and down the sidewalk in front of West High School carrying signs which said that black cheerleaders may cheer too, black teachers, we want black teachers for black history courses. They walked up and down in a peaceful and orderly fashion. And then the police came, they turned on their loudspeakers, read their ordinances over the loudspeakers and started to arrest people. And the facts in this case show that that's when it appeared that people started to watch what was going on. But under 19.2, your clients would have been found guilty of willfully making or assisting in the making of any noise or diversion which disturbs or tends to disturb the peace or good order, were they not? That's correct, your honor, and I submit that that language is vague and it does not comport with the standards of due process of law and giving due notice to the persons who wish to comply with the law and who at the same time wish to exercise their First Amendment freedom does not give them an opportunity to exercise them because they don't know what they're going to be arrested for. Your attack on that section of the ordinance is not based on the First Amendment but on grounds of vagueness? Your honor, it's also based on the First Amendment because by its vagueness which violates due process, it is subject to an overbroad application to perfectly protected constitutional freedom. You would, uh, what would be your view of the statute prohibiting picketing on the sidewalks adjacent to this building? Unconstitutional? Unconstitutional. I would have to, the people who drafted the statute, what would be their purpose in drafting it? What state interest would they want to protect? Would they want to protect this court from being disturbed? The statute in Cox v. Louisiana concerned one that was narrowly drawn which said we will prohibit picketing of persons who seek to disturb, I don't have the exact language of it, disturb the processes of the administration of justice? In that particular instance, where the court is concerned and where the statute is so narrowly drawn as this court held it was, I would say that it was... Do you think it's unreasonable then for a legislature, a lawmaking body, to conclude that as many people as you have here, 200, has the tendency to disturb the educational process? I think Justice Stewart made the appropriate statement when he wrote this court's opinion in Tinker v. Des Moines. He said there must be a substantial showing that there would be an interference with the orderly process of the school administration. There has been no such showing in this particular case, Your Honor. As a matter of fact, I think it is important, and I am in accord with this decision, is it important that students in our schools be allowed to see and to participate in exercising the First Amendment freedoms so that in the school they're not only taught the three R's, but they're also taught how to be citizens in this country and how to exercise their rights as guaranteed by the First Amendment. May I ask, for what was the penalty to the post? Mr. Green, it was fined $25 for violating 18.1i and $25 for violating 19.2a, plus court clause. That's different from the other case. The what case? The other case that's involved here. In the most of the case, there was no arrest, there was no conviction, there was no fine. His was a declaratory judgment action. My client has been... But at least the other action concerns only one ordinance. The other action, that's right. Mine concerns two... Two ordinance. Right, 19.2a being the second ordinance. 19.2a has no exemption for labor unions. No, it does not. It applies to any person. Do you think it's a denial of equal protection if the law-making body of crops? A labor dispute is entitled to a higher order of picketing rights than just any other people. Yes, I do. And I also would say that it is significant in my particular case that the city of Rockford has eliminated the labor picketing distinction. Now, Section 18.1i is just that all labor picketing, all picketing completely is prohibited within 150 feet, which shows that at the time this ordinance was applied to my client, it not only is an admission by the city that it not only violated the Constitution, but or it shows that obviously the labor picketing exemption had no compelling state interest to warrant it being there. So at the time this ordinance was applied to my client, the city admits that it violated the Constitution. I don't suppose the city would agree with you that the change in the ordinance has that meaning and only that meaning, you know, would... I would presume that they would bring forth some other reason, but I submit that this change at this time shows that it has no compelling state interest. I wanted to make a point about 19.2a. I already have mentioned that I think it violates due notice because the person can't know what conduct is prohibited. So even if he is trying to comply with the laws at the same time exercises constitutional rights, he does not have an opportunity to do. Consequently, he cannot act at all without fear of going to jail. The other point is that with respect to 19.2a, as the ordinance is drafted, it says that a person who willfully makes a noise of diversion would violate that section. And then it seems to modify that which disturbs or tends to disturb the peace and good order of the school session. I submit that what is happening is that the person is being convicted when he makes a noise of diversion, and his intent is just to make the noise of diversion, not to disturb or disturb the peace and good order of the school session. I don't know what I'm going to say. I'm going to leave with us. Is there evidence in that, that there was noise? Yes, there's evidence, Your Honor. But the evidence shows that the noise came from the use of the police loudspeakers. I don't know what I'm going to ask you. Is there any evidence that there was any noise by the group whom you represent? How many were there? Forty eyes? I, there were 200 demonstrators who were in front of the school. Forty males were arrested. And I represented those. Is there any evidence that those Forty? My client, Richard Grainett. No, there's no evidence with respect to Richard Grainett, because as you can see from the common law record, Richard Grainett was not charged and convicted of making a noise. He was charged and convicted of making a diversion. So with respect to him. What's the evidence that he made a diversion? I submit the record to this court to find it. You mean there's none in it? That's your suggestion. As far as I can see, there's no... Is there Thompson in Louisville? That's your suggestion. I, we had not raised that argument in our brief, your honor. I would suggest that there was noise at the scene, and the noise came when the loudspeakers were used by the police officers. Whatever that may be. Is there any affirmative evidence that you're, the only one we have here is Mr. Grainett. Mr. Grainett, that's right. Any evidence at all on this record that he was noisy? He was making a noise? That he committed a diversion? There's no evidence that he was noisy, and I, I am just, I would say there was no evidence that he personally, personally, himself was making a diversion. Now whether they would consider assisting in the entire demonstration that they made a diversion, I would say there's no evidence for that because I say that the record will show that at the time there was evidence of a large number of people standing in the windows at the school, it was after the loudspeakers were used by the police in reading the ordinances to them. Ms. Hall, you didn't raise any Thompson versus Louisville point in the Supreme Court of Illinois. No, I did not, sir. You said 40 were arrested. There were 40 demonstrators who were arrested. Well, were they all convicted? The, um... I mean, is this a symbolic case or what? Because it's... Because there were 40 cases... The case is brought here as the one that has no record as to what the man did. And that's the record I'm bringing with you now. Which, there's nothing in there to show that he did anything. That he... There is evidence in there that he participated in the demonstration, but there's nothing in my judgment to show that the diversions were committed by the demonstrators. Is there anything in the record that shows that this man has drained, drained, opened his mouth, said anything? I, um... I wouldn't be surprised if he said something, Your Honor, and I don't know what the record shows exactly to his making comments to the people around him. Well, I'll read. I submit that I am here for Richard Drainett, and I'm asking this court to sustain the faith for the citizens of Rockford that this court will protect their right to exercise their freedoms, which are protected from state interference through the 14th Amendment. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Hall. Mr. Curry? Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. The issues of this case as viewed by the City of Chicago are three. Does the claim of a free man to use the streets as a public forum exclude even modest regulations as to the time and place within which its rights may be exercised? Two, if modest regulations are permissible in protecting substantial governmental interest, is Chicago in error in ascribing such importance to its schools? And three, is the Chicago ordinance void by reason of being overbroad? The City of Chicago believes that the rule of this case ought to answer each question in the negative. The ordinance before the court is a partial restriction as to picketing and demonstrating around elementary and secondary schools. Reasonable as to time, that is, during classes and a half hour before and after, and reasonable, I submit, as to place, that is, within 150 feet of the school building. When local government is attempting to harmonize and accommodate conflicting demands for the use of streets, the standards as to time and place are every bit as relevant as the controls upon manner and purpose. This ordinance ought not be viewed as a ban on First Amendment rights. It is clearly and properly a phasing or timing of the activities in recognition that at a certain time and within a certain limited area, there does exist competing interests which the City may rightly acknowledge and regulate. The purpose of the ordinance and the reason for its passage and the reason for the phasing and timing contained in it is that the City sought to impose a very simple ordinance on school picketing. and the City Council sought to assure that school kids have a setting for education where tranquility, order, calm and quiet might prevail or at least not be minimized by introducing picketing or demonstrating and their customary counterparts. Adderley v. Florida tells us that there may be some public places which are so clearly committed to other purposes that their use for airing grievances is anomalous. In Adderley, it was the private driveway to the jail. In Cox v. Louisiana, it was near a courthouse. In Cameron v. Johnson, it was access to public buildings. Chicago believes that the schoolhouse ought to receive similar insulation from what has been traditionally described as speech plus activities while classes are in session. the ordinance in Chicago was passed in response to widespread and ugly demonstrations which were taking place on a daily basis at elementary schools where black students were being bussed for the first time. The respondent, Mosley, would have this court believe that an ordinance with such a derivation was merely a ploy for stifling his cry for a larger black enrollment at Jones Commercial High School. Mr. Curry, you said that you're trying to do the same thing that was done in Cox. Yes, sir. And it appears from the decision of the Bill's facing decision that that's just the point. You said what Cox said it would be valid. Isn't that what he said? The court found the ordinance of the city of Chicago to be overbroad and answered no further questions than an issue. Justice Marshall. It's my recollection. He said that it was because it was narrowly drawn to protect a valid state influence. That's what he said. You're reading from Cox, sir. No, sir. I'm reading from Judge Hastings. Judge, it's my recollection. I'm certainly going to quarrel with your reading of the order, sir. The court's order, my interpretation was, it was strictly and solely on overbreath that it did classify... If you'd written one of my Cox, he would have upheld it. That's what I gather from this. We submit, Justice Marshall, that this is very narrow. This ordinance is narrow and is not vague. The ordinance is precisely drawn and patently designed to accomplish its objectives. It thus fits the court's off-repeated description of the kind of law that should be drawn in the state's exercise of generally unquestioned constitutional power to regulate picketing and street activity. The ordinance does, as Thornhill directs us, aim specifically at evils within the allowable area of state control and does not leave one to guess at where fanciful possibilities end and intended coverage begins. Why the exception then for labor picketing? Mr. Justice Brennan, the exemption for labor picketing has its derivation in these facts. The primary goal of this legislation was public issue picketing. That was the question that the city of Chicago was confronted with on its streets at the time this ordinance came up. There was then none, nor had there been in the memory of those in the city council any public school labor picketing at all. You don't suggest that labor picketing, particularly when it involves school teachers, it's not a publication picket. Yes, but public picketing when it, in Illinois, when it involves school teachers or school employees, public employees generally, is determined by the rule of law in Illinois that that picketing is contrary to public policy and can be enjoined by state action. Well, what kind of ticketing is you going to have around school? You would have the kind that could be enjoined by appropriate state action. A remedy being available to meet this possibility, the city of Chicago felt in drawing a very narrow ordinance, we would only relate our ordinance to the experiences that were then prevalent in the streets.
